text:
The 2022 UK pilot ran for six months across 61 companies and about 2,900 employees. Of those companies, 56 kept the shorter schedule, and revenue barely dropped.

These numbers make the idea look better than it may be, because the firms chose to take part. Volunteers tend to be knowledge-work companies, and their calendars are full of meetings that are easy to cut.

Iceland's public-sector trials, which ran from 2015 to 2019 and covered about 2,500 workers, point to a different source of the benefit. The gain seems to come less from working fewer hours than from being forced to review the calendar. Leaders had long paid a "Friday tax" of low-value meetings and finally stopped paying it.

Teams should pilot a four-day week where value is defined by output, not by being present. Customer support rotations and on-call incident response plans rarely survive a shorter week without extra staff.

Here is a simple test. If a team cannot cut enough meetings to fit into 32 hours within one quarter, the four-day week becomes a pay cut disguised as a perk.
